  residual: accepted; alert when disk is over 80 percent
  owner: platform team
blocks.caption: Every row names the element, the response, how it is done, and the test or owner that keeps it true. That is what question 4 checks.

blocks.title: Risk per threat, before and after (High 3, Medium 2, Low 1)

scenes.caption: Before: four High threats. T2 and T8 are High because they need no special skill and expose everything; T1 because leaked passwords are cheap.
After the responses: everything Low except T6, deliberately accepted at Medium with an alert. Each rating still has a written reason behind it.

blocks.md:
**Question 4: did we do a good enough job?** Shostack's checklist: does the model match what was built, did each threat get the right response, and is there a test? In practice:

- Redraw the DFD from the deployed system (routes, buckets, accounts), not from memory, and compare.
- For each mitigated threat, write a test that fails if the fix is removed.
- For each accepted threat, check that the owner and the alert exist.
- Put the model in code review: any change that adds an element, a flow or a trust boundary crossing reopens question 1.

blocks.code:
# tests/test_authz.py: the test that keeps T2 fixed (Python, pytest)
def test_cannot_read_other_users_note(client, make_user, make_note, login):
    alice, bob = make_user("alice"), make_user("bob")
    note = make_note(owner=alice, body="private")
    login(client, bob)
    for path in (f"/notes/{note.id}", f"/export/{note.id}"):
        resp = client.get(path)
        assert resp.status_code == 404, path    # same answer as a missing note
blocks.caption: Answering 404 rather than 403 also avoids confirming that the note exists. The loop covers both routes that take a note id today. A new route is only tested once it is added to the tuple, so list routes from the router or add each one here.

blocks.md: A good threat model is small, specific and alive: a diagram that matches the system, a short list of threats with a response, a reason and a test for each, and a habit of reopening it whenever the design changes.

blocks.question: Notely adds a feature: users can import notes from a URL, and the API fetches that URL. Which threat-model step comes first?
options: Add a firewall rule
Return to question 1: add the new outbound flow and the external servers it reaches to the diagram, then run STRIDE on them
Score the feature with DREAD
Accept the risk because the API already has authentication
blocks.explain: A new flow and a new external entity change the diagram, so question 1 reopens. The API fetching arbitrary URLs from inside your network is a new trust boundary crossing. Fixes and scores come after the threats are found.

blocks.question: Which pair of threats did BOTH the attack tree and STRIDE per element flag as the cheapest or most urgent?
options: T5 and T7
T4 and T6
T8 and T9
T1 (password replay) and T2 (IDOR)
blocks.explain: The attack tree's cheapest branches were password replay (200) and the URL trick (500); the ratings of the STRIDE threat list put both at High. Agreement between two techniques raises confidence that the obvious threats are covered.

blocks.md:
**Practise legally.** Test only systems you own or have written permission to test (security-basics covers the law). Good next steps:

- [OWASP Threat Dragon](https://owasp.org/www-project-threat-dragon/): a free tool for drawing DFDs with trust boundaries and recording STRIDE threats. Model an app you have built.
- [Elevation of Privilege](https://shostack.org/games/elevation-of-privilege): Adam Shostack's threat modeling card game, organised around STRIDE, for practising question 2 with a team.
- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy, access control](https://portswigger.net/web-security/access-control): free labs where you find the IDOR and missing-check bugs from lessons 7 and 9 in deliberately vulnerable apps.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/): a deliberately insecure shop to run locally. Threat model it first, then check your list against what you find.
